utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Unfortunately, as you can see, Judge Van den Wyngaert is not able to sit again this afternoon but, we believe, will be with us tomorrow, so we will sit under 15 bis. Mr. Saxon, have you a matter that arises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Your Honour. The Prosecution understands that the cross-examination of the current witness will continue for some time, and it is obvious that it involves a number of issues, some of which are complex. And the Prosecution would simply like to ask that my colleagues on the Defence side ensure that before they sit down and complete their cross-examinations, that they comply with the Rule 90(h)(2) which requires a cross-examining party to put clearly to the person being cross-examined the nature of the accused's case which is in contradiction to the evidence of the witness. I'd simply like to place that on the record, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you like us to respond, Your Honour? I don't see the need, but if directed by the Court ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I had not thought you would need to respond.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I don't see any need, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a provision of the Rule. We would have assumed you would be complying with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We hope we are, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can we have in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Once again, the affirmation you made at the beginning is still applicable. And sorry that you were delayed. There was a small procedural matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, once again, a question about general practice and procedure followed by your organisation in the course of your investigation. Is that correct that it is the practice of your organisation, when an individual alleges an abuse of his right, to seek to obtain court files or court records, if available?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, can you rephrase your question? I'm not sure I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sure. Perhaps what I'll do is I'll read to you the proposition from your colleague, Mr. Abrahams, when he was asked the same question. He was asked to explain the methodology of your organisation in relation to this matter. It's 1D00-3927. It's Rule 65 ter 1D429. It's Prosecution v. Milosevic of the 3rd June 2002, page 6054. He was asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Human rights methodology, please, very shortly. The Chamber will be familiar with the general proposition, but we just need on the record what the methodology is." And the answer of Mr. Abrahams was the following: "The primary source for the -- of information for the organisation is fieldwork, that is, interviews with the victims and witnesses of abuse. We conduct interviews with these people, lengthy, in-depth interviews, in a one-on-one setting whenever possible, and we search for corroborative evidence. If someone has had illegal -- is alleging illegal violation, we ask for court records. If they ask -- if they are alleging physical abuse recently, we ask to see scars or bruises. We also collect documents from medical -- medical records, government reports and so on. Whenever possible, we also try to visit crime scenes or the sites of the alleged violations, and we also try to get information from alleged perpetrators." Is that a fair description of the usual practice of your organisation, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a fair description, although I think when Mr. Abrahams was speaking about the legal violation, he was talking about our work monitoring court proceedings and inquests, and in those cases we would be asking for -- or we would try to obtain or monitor the court proceedings directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is it correct also that in this particular case, the case of Ljuboten, you've made no request to receive any court documents or any court files? You had no reason to do so; is that what you answered previously?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you made no requests to receive any medical records, either; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that you have no forensic training or no forensic expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask you to make pauses. Our languages are less concise, and we need time to pronounce things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert is being better than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question, Mr. Bouckaert?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm just pausing until the blinker stops blinking, as I've been instructed to. I don't have any formal forensic training. We do have forensic training at Human Rights Watch which is conducted by eminent forensic experts such as Mr. Bill Hagland of Physicians for Human Rights, Mr. Eric Stoffer, who helped the OTP set up its forensic programme, I've also worked with Dr. Helena Hrunta [phoen] of the Helsinki Forensic Institute, so I do believe in the course of my work, in the course of these internal Human Rights Watch trainings, which I helped set up, that I have developed a basic forensic experience as it relates to my work. I've also written extensively about forensic issues related to the 2003 Iraq war. I wrote a report about the mass graves of Mah Weil [phoen] and how the lack of forensic programmes in place was destroying important evidence in Iraq.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let me read that to you, if I may, Mr. Bouckaert. It's again an answer of your colleague Mr. Abrahams. This time it's from the Milatinovic case. It's Rule 65 ter 1D424, and it's at page 1D00-3813. That's Prosecutor v. Milatinovic, and it's at page 920. The date is 14th of July of 2006. It's again Mr. Abrahams who was being asked about forensic and ballistic. And if I may draw your attention, it's at line 9, what would be -- line 9, yes, I'm grateful. It says this, that's the answer of your colleague: "Both Mr. Bouckaert and I have extensive experience operating in war zones, and as part of that we conduct investigations, multipronged investigations. The essential element is the interview, as I've mentioned, but in addition we survey the scene, we draw a map of the environment, we look at the physical evidence to determine what took place. We do not conduct extensive forensic examination because we do not have that expertise." Is that a correct assessment of yours and Mr. Abrahams' expertise in forensic matters?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the operative word here is we do not conduct extensive forensic examinations as would be done by a forensic pathologist in a laboratory. However, we certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, you --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I finish my answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are certainly able to assess basic forensic evidence to assess wounds received during beatings and to tell the difference between an entry an exit wound, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But to answer my previous question, and I think it can be answered quite easily, you do not have any forensic training or expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I said I partook in an internal forensic training programme at Human Rights Watch, and I have worked with forensic experts in the field, so I certainly have some limited forensic training.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you consider that is sufficient to consider --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down and make breaks. Please make breaks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, your answer was -- your question was --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I was simply asking you whether, contrary to what Mr. Abrahams suggested, it was the last part of the sentence that was of interest to me, where he says: "... Because we do not have that expertise." You disagree with his assessment, and you are claiming that you have forensic expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm waiting for the question to finish appearing on my screen. I don't disagree with what Mr. Abrahams has said. He said, we do not have the expertise, quote, "conduct extensive forensic examinations." With that, I totally agree. I do think as field researchers, we do have the expertise to make basic forensic assessments.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. And is that correct that this is the basics that you used to make a number of findings in relation to what you believe to be injuries sustained to a number of people you have interviews -- interviewed, I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you also made a number of findings as to what happened to a number of deceased persons but also to a number of people that had been injured based not on your own observations but on what you were told by others; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And on a number of occasions, you did not seek to verify in any way the statements which were given to you by a number of villagers as to how they incurred injuries or as to how a particular individual had been killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll draw your attention to your report, which is P352. And if I could ask the Registry kindly to go to page 10 of that report. There's a sentence I would like to draw your attention upon. It's in the paragraph -- inside the paragraph which starts with the word: "Two of the bodies were found ..." Can you locate this one?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll just read, I think, the third sentence. It says: "Sulleyman Bajrami was found face down in the road, shot in the head and chest and with a large head wound." Then you go on to say: " Empty 99-millimetre cartridges were lying next to Bajrami's body, and bloody tracks were from an armoured personnel carrier, APC, suggested that his body had been run over by a Macedonian APC." Can you tell this Chamber what is the basis for your belief that the body of Mr. Bajrami had been run over by a Macedonian APC?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was -- all of this information was based on a large number of photographs that I was able to review, as well as the field notes of one of the international journalists who had been at the scene on August 14th, as well as my personal visit later on on August 23rd. So it was a combination of those pieces of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And on that basis, you were satisfied that you could conclude that the body in question had indeed been run over by an APC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not the entire body, but we believe that part of the body had been run over by an APC, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown the consolidated statement of Mr. Bolton. This is ERN N00-6468-0. It's a "P" exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, what I'm -- I'm grateful. This is the consolidated statement of Mr. Bolton, which I understand you know, worked for the OSCE in Macedonia at that time, and I'd ask the Registry to move to page 12 of this statement and focus on paragraph 15, 1-5. Were you aware, sir, of the fact that Mr. Bolton had been in the village on the 14th of August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you look at paragraph 15 of that statement, that's what Mr. Bolton, who saw the bodies in the village on that day, said: "I was told by local inhabitants that his body had been run over by an armoured vehicle," and he's talking about the same body as you did: "However, I do not believe this to be correct, as the body did not have any obvious crush-type injury that I could see. I do believe, due to tire marks on the road, that a large vehicle did travel down the road from east to west, passing through the blood spilled close to the body. There was no indication that the vehicle had moved through the blood spill travelling west to east." So you would agree that, at least according to Mr. Bolton, who personally observed the body of Mr. Bajrami and who, the paragraph suggests, consulted it quite carefully and concluded that the body had not been run over by an APC; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if Mr. Bolton is to be believed, that would make your finding quite wrong; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this one single point, there would be a disagreement, yes. When I visited the village, I saw the large blood stain on the street with the APC having run through it, so my own visual inspection of the scene would not be that different from Mr. Bolton, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you didn't see the body; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but there's a photograph of the body in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the photograph was enough for you to draw that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And in any case, it would be rather a marginal conclusion in terms of our assessment of the nature of the crime. Our assessment of the nature of the crime committed against Mr. Sulleyman Bajrami did not relate to him being run over by an APC. It related to him being shot dead in a summary manner by the Macedonian police.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreters kindly ask you again for pauses and to slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct, sir, that in your statement to the Office of the Prosecution, you indicated that you had observed what you believed to be cigarette burns on the body of Mr. Qaili?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And again this is a finding which you based on what you said were your forensic expertise; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on my very brief inspection of the body which took place as the funeral of Mr. Qaili was taking place at his house, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you did not seek to obtain medical confirmation of that fact; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you were aware at the time that Mr. Qaili had been autopsied; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he had a large scar down the middle of his chest.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you would agree that if the doctors or the professors who treated -- that wouldn't be a good expression, but who autopsied Mr. Qaili were to give evidence that there were no such burns, cigarette burns or otherwise on the body of Mr. Qaili, that would again be quite a significant discrepancy with your evidence?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I would not necessarily place a whole lot of faith in the autopsy reports of those doctors. We have documented, not in Macedonia but certainly in Kosovo, autopsy reports which failed to acknowledge that people had been beaten to death and tortured in police custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, do you have any such information in relation to Skopje Forensic institute?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I would just treat the evidence with some caution.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct that you've indicated to me that you've interviewed approximately 35 villagers or so in the context of your investigation, approximately?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I said that I didn't have an exact number, but I would estimate it was between 35 and 40, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would be during a period of about seven days; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make the breaks and slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that you took an average of an hour to two hours per witness, per interview; would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would depend on the nature of the interview. Many of those interviews would be quite shorter, but certainly for the key witnesses, they would be of that period of time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that all of those interviews were conducted from English into Albanian and from Albanian back into English through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them, yes. There were a few which were conducted directly in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that this would mean that effectively the length of the interview would be between half an hour and an hour, accounting for the translation of the question and the answers?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviews took as long as it took to get as complete an account as possible from the witness. I don't want to speculate on those kind of divisions of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I don't think it was a speculation. You would agree that considering that the questions and the answer had to be translated back and forth, that would mean that effectively the interview was between, on average, between 30 minutes and one hour; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interviews took as long as they took to get a complete account -- as complete account as possible from the witness. So there was no time limits on the interviews. It depended on the amount of information the witness had and the time period that we were talking about. Some witnesses we only interviewed about events which took 10, 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'll just kindly ask you at this stage if you can answer my questions as concisely and as precisely as you can. If there's a need for explanation, I will either ask you a question or my colleague will do so. We're under time pressure to try to finish today. I'd be grateful. Is that also correct that the information that you've put in your report, and you've indicated that this was evidence which you believe to be sufficiently reliable or sufficiently corroborated to be aired in public; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a few questions about a number of villagers which you interviewed in the course of your investigation. The first such person is Mr. Qani Jashari, and I would like again the Registry, please, to bring up the report prepared by Mr. Bouckaert. It's P352. At page 11 of the report, that would be U0000108. I'd like you to focus on the first full paragraph, Mr. Bouckaert, with the words starting: "The police reportedly ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll just read it out to you. It says: "The police reportedly continued down Rastak Road burning the garage of Ali Aliu and then shooting up the house up of Aziz Bajrami. They then reached the house of 65-year-old Qani Jashari who was hiding inside with two of his sons, 33-year-old Bajram and 31-year-old Kadri, as well as a cousin, 25-year-old Xhelal Bajrami, a son of Aziz Bajrami. The police officers began firing with RPGs and automatic weapons at the house, causing it to catch on fire. Qani Jashari escaped to a nearby ditch, but the three young men were gunned down while trying to escape from the burning home." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there's a passage which is somewhat indented. Do I understand that this is essentially a verbatim record of what Mr. Qani Jashari told you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then I'll read that to you. It says: "The police first surrounded us. I went to hide in a pipe nearby. The boys remained in the house trying to hide. They started shelling the house with grenades and from their APCs. Then the house caught on fire from the grenade. It was made out of wood. When the fire started, the boys climbed out through a window. They ran away, but the police started shooting at them. The police were in the yard, maybe 30 or 40 of them, with their APCs. After the boys were shot, four or five police walked up to them. They went to the farthest one. He was about 20 metres further away than the two others. He had run fastest. It was Kadri. They turned him around. He was lying on his stomach, and they turned him on his back. He was still moving. They shot him again in the neck. Then they took his documents. I later found them by the road." And then there's a footnote and you refer to the interview with Mr. Qani Jashari which you had in Skopje in August of 2001; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that you presented Mr. Qani Jashari, in your statement and in this report as well, and that's paragraph 72 of your statement as having been an eyewitness to these killings?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you obtain or did you seek, rather, any corroboration of Mr. Jashari's information?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you obtain any?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you identify the person who gave you information about that matter?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the field notes of journalist Nicholas Wood of the "The Guardian" who had visited Ljuboten on the 14th and who had obtained similar accounts from the witnesses in the village, which was not Mr. Qani Jashari.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, that was my next question. Is that correct that Mr. Wood obtained his information also from the villagers?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you seek to obtain corroboration from any of the villagers yourself to verify this story?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During my own visit to Ljuboten, I was told a similar account without any discrepancies by the villagers who accompanied me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you consider the evidence of Mr. Jashari to be reliable and sufficiently verified to be reprinted in that manner in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just me but also the people who reviewed the report prior to publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And Mr. Jashari did not mention at any stage that fire had been coming from his house at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, and neither did our own physical inspection of the area find any evidence of fire from the home.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he did not mention escaping the house with his son Afet; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him mentioning his son Afet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is now P350, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, you've just indicated that your physical inspection of the house did not reveal any evidence of fire from the home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If you look at the picture, is that correct that the incoming fire, so to say, was directed at the upper floor of the house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but on this side and on the front side of the home.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, let's stick with this side for the time being. You would agree that the fire, the incoming fire, is directed at the upper floor of the house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that the roof and ceiling of the upper floor tumbled down during the incident; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I've made clear in my direct testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that also correct that you could not, therefore, visit the upper floor of the house to look for traces of outgoing fire?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The inside of the house was in rubble inside, so we focused -- we did look inside to see if there were any spent bullet casings, which would have been near the top of the rubble if they did come from that second floor, and we also focused on looking at the structures nearby and any trees to see if there was any evidence of outgoing gunfire.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But on top of the floor, the second floor, it would be a roof, isn't it, an entire layer coming through the roof, is that correct, so you would have to dig through the rubbles of the roof and try to locate casings; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as you can see from the front of the house, the tiles in front, we're not talking about a very thick layer of tiles, and certainly we did not remove all of those tiles and carry out a complete investigation of the floors of the homes, but we did look around to see if there was any evidence of sand-bagging or spent bullet cases inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And how long did you spend digging through the rubbles of the house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't really dig through the rubble. We walked through the rubble to see if there was anything visible for, I would say, about 10 or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that you didn't ask the Macedonian authorities, whether it is the police or the army, whether they had any information in relation to that particular house and, in particular, whether anyone would have seen outgoing fire from that house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask, and as far as I know, no allegations were made by the Macedonian authorities, either in the local or the international press, or by holding any press conferences to suggest that there had been outgoing fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is identified as Exhibit 1D87. It's 1D00-3979 and 1D00-3977 in the Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, this is again the same document that I have showed you briefly yesterday, and it comes from the UBK, the Security and Counter-Intelligence Division of the Ministry of Interior at Cair. And if may ask the Registry again to turn to the second page, the next page. I would just like to draw your attention again to the same paragraph, where it says: "At the end of the meeting, Odza informed that the houses which are most damaged in areas of Skamala in the village of Ljuboten are the ones from which that the security forces of the Republic of Macedonia were fired upon by the residents of the aforementioned quarter and that according to him this is the reason why the majority of those killed are residents of that quarter; that is, the houses of Veseli Avdi, Jashari Aziz, Bajrami Qani, and the Zendeli family are located there." Is that correct that refers inter alia to the house of Aziz Jashari, also known as Aziz Bajrami?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the report refers to, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Your Honour, we would like to tender this document at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification. Can my colleague tell us when and where this particular document was obtained, and particularly if it was obtained from an archive, which archive?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I certainly can, Your Honour. This is the same source as has been used by the Prosecution in particular in the report of Mr. Beserokenko. It is the same archive, the UBK archives, which has led the Prosecution to making a recent application for an admission of documents from the same source. I can't remember the date off the top of my head, Your Honour, the date which we received the document, but if there is any need to receive a formal letter from the source, we could certainly do so. But in effect it's the same source used by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not objecting to the admission of the document. It would simply be helpful to the Prosecution if we could be informed of the date when this document was provided to the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We will provide this indication, Your Honour, to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mettraux. The document will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D87, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, there is another document which I would like to show you, and it is 1D24. It is a report prepared by the OSCE. It's a special report on the Ljuboten incident. And I will come back to the report in a moment. At this stage, there are two particular parts that I would wish to show you. As you can see, it is dated the 16th of August, 2001. It is a special report on the Ljuboten incident. I'd kindly ask the Registry to turn to the next page. And if the paragraph started with the words: "In contrast ..." could be somewhat enlarged for Mr. Bouckaert. It would be the fourth paragraph from the top. I'll read the paragraph to you, Mr. Bouckaert. It says: "In contrast to the situation with the two men in town, the three men, whose bodies were found unevenly spaced apart in a field on the edge of town, appear to have been fleeing uphill from the edge of the village at the time they were killed. With regard to these persons, because of all of the information available to the mission, there is a general sense that their deaths are less suspicious and possibly related to legitimate military action. That cannot be said of the aforementioned two persons who were found in the residential area. As to the two men in town, the question seems more likely to be who is responsible, not whether there is something to be responsible for." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if I can ask the Registry to turn to page 4 of that document and to focus on the paragraph starting with the words: "Near the field ..." that would be the third paragraph from the top or the fourth. I'll just read to you the last two sentences of that paragraph. It says: "The building on the left," and they are talking of the same groups of buildings, "the buildings on the left have been burned and have been the subject of considerable incoming weapon fire. These buildings are located where they could be a useful observation point from which to monitor Macedonian movement or directing fire upon them." Is that an observation you would agree with?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Now I'd like to show you another part of the -- to put to you another part of the evidence which has been given in this case. One particular witness who was called earlier by the Prosecution was asked to describe his observation concerning that set of houses, and this is what he said. Your Honour, this is Witness M-84 on the date of the 25th of May, 2007. It's at page 1494-1495, and it says this: "I wanted to ask you whether in the morning, as you headed out with your chief, Mr. Karstevski [phoen], whether you noted that there was gunfire coming from one of the houses in Ljuboten and whether, in your preparation for this evidence, you were actually able to show this house to the Prosecution." The witness said: "I saw this. At this moment, what it was about, where the people were, I can't say, because from Radisani you can't see Ljuboten because there is a hill. Radisani is down in a hole." He says: "When I climbed up there, that is what I can see. I can't say some hearsay that there was some shooting or something. It would not be appropriate for me to say -- to speak about hearsay. I will only speak about what I have seen with my own eyes." Then he was asked: "And the house from which you were able to see the gunfire, you pinpointed it on a picture for the Prosecution when you arrived here in The Hague; is that correct? "It is correct. When I went off that house and that elevation, you can see the positions of Ljubanci, the positions that were there, the police positions, the check-points. One could see a reflection of fire of automatic rifles. I don't know whether other weapons, but you could see fire. It was some two kilometres away but through the binoculars one could see that one -- one was shooting from one side to the other side there." And what this witness pinpointed to in proofing with the Prosecution was, in fact, the house owned by the Jashari family, and my question is: Did you have that information at the time or did you seek to obtain that information?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour. I would simply ask that the question be phrased in a form that is accurate. The use of the word "pinpointed," in my recollection, is a rather broad description of a circle that Witness M-84 drew around a series of houses or a neighbourhood during his evidence, and so I'm just wondering whether my colleague might want to consider rephrasing that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I think I can assist, Your Honour. I'll read verbatim from the notes taken and given to us by the Prosecution. It's the proofing notes of the 20th of May of 2007, Witness M-84: "In the morning on 12 August 2001, I was on an observation point along the road from Ljuboten leading to Skopje. On a small elevation near the area where the garbage is dumped outside Ljuboten. From where -- from there, I could observe some gunfire coming out of houses on the side of the village bordering Rastak." And then there is a note by the Prosecution, and it says: "When the witness was asked to indicate these houses on a photograph of Ljuboten, the witness pointed to the house known to the Prosecution as the houses owned by the Jashari family. The witness did not indicate that he knew who owned this house. The witness did not know who was firing from this house." So perhaps I can put my question to you again, Mr. Bouckaert. Did you, at the time, have that information and did you seek to obtain that information from the authorities?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I have noted earlier that you represented in your report, and also in your statement, the evidence of Mr. Qani Jashari as being that of an eyewitness, is that correct, to the killing of his son; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- I don't think we used the word "eyewitness." We say "witness." But he did -- he did witness the incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, at paragraph 72 of your Prosecution statement, you say this: "On 20 August 2001 in Skopje, I had interviewed the father of two of the killed man, Qani Jashari, who had been an eyewitness of the event." Is that --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd ask the Registry's assistant to bring up Rule 65 ter 2D32 with an ERN 2D00-0454. There is no Macedonian, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, this is the -- a statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor by Mr. Qani Jashari on the 7th of October of 2004, and I would ask, with the Registry's assistance, to go immediately to page 3 of that statement and to focus on the last paragraph on that page. That's paragraph 17. In this paragraph, Mr. Bouckaert, Mr. Qani Jashari says this: "I and my son Afet were leaving from my house down the gravel path to the road. I decided to go this way because I was too old to run uphill. Afet was ahead of me. The rest of the family stayed in the house." And you've indicated earlier that, in fact, Mr. Jashari did not mention his son Afet to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would ask the Registry to now turn to the next page, and that's page 4, and to focus, please, on paragraph 19. And then he said: "On the road, I separated from Afet, crossed the street, and hided myself in bushes directly beside the road, on the south side of the road. Since I was afraid they would spot me, I crawled further downhill. It was a piece of around 20 to 30 metres open grass." You would agree that Mr. Jashari told the Prosecution that he hid not in a pipe, as he told you, but in bushes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that stage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then if I can draw your attention to what he says in paragraph 20. He said: "I reached a bunch of bushes in which I hided myself until the police withdrew from the area. From these bushes, I could see parts of the road. I couldn't see what was going on in my house and at the new houses. My position was too low to have a clear sight." Do you agree that at this stage, as you point out, he couldn't see what was going on near the house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If I can ask the Registry to turn to the next page, page 5, and to focus on paragraph 30, please. Paragraph 30 says: "Soon afterwards, the house started to burn. I could see the flames coming up, but like I said before, my sight was very limited. I could not see what was going on the ground."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in fact what he's saying there again is he could not see what was going on in front of the house and in the house; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I guess so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If we can go to paragraph 33, which is further down. It says: "Short after the police disappeared, Afet and myself left nearly at the same time our hiding places. At this I learned that Afet was hiding himself in the bushes north of the road close to the gravel path to my house." And then he says: "We approached the house and were looking for some leftover from my sons. At this moment, I was convinced that there were only two options, either they were killed inside the house and burnt or they were running away." And then he says: "After we didn't find anything in the house, Afet went down to the Ametovski house in order to join with the rest of the family which were at this time in the area of the stream. He was thinking that Kadri and Bajrami had obviously escaped." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And again that indicates, doesn't it, that contrary to what Mr. Jashari told you, he didn't see the killing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a different account from what he gave us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Then if I can draw your attention to paragraph 36. It says: "After Afet left the place, I found the bodies in the field. Being asked for the time, I say it was around late afternoon." So you will agree that the story that Mr. Jashari gave to the Prosecution is, as you pointed out, quite different than the story that he gave you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are some significant differences in the account, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Including the fact that he didn't witness the killing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see where it says that he directly witnessed the killing in our report, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I've just read to you the passage where you said, in your statement, that he had been an eyewitness to the killing. Would you like me to read it again to you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I agree that I said in my statement that he was an eyewitness, but I don't see where, in our report, it says that he directly witnessed the killings.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, your statement says this: "On 20 August 2001 in Skopje, I had interviewed the father of two of the killed men, Qani Jashari, who had been an eyewitness of the event." That's your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you go on to say: "His testimony is on page 11 of the report." And that's the evidence that you gave to the Prosecution, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if we go on, is it also correct that he could not see what was happening, or he told the Prosecution, in any case, that he could not see what was happening in and around the house other than the flames coming out of the house, is that correct, that's the version that he gave to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he also told them -- or he did not claim to the Prosecution that he could see his sons climbing out of the windows, like he had told you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I just see the next paragraph of his statement, actually, the -- where he talks about Kadri's body?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Certainly. I will come to the issue of Kadri, Mr. Bouckaert, but which paragraph would you like to --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to see the rest of paragraph 39.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the Registry assist? I'll read it out to you: "Afterwards, I wanted to drag the body of Kadri down. At this moment I heard from the check-point somebody screaming, 'Are you still alive,' and then they started to shoot at my direction. Being asked from what distance this voice came, I say this was far away, maybe 2.000 metres or closer. It came from the check-point of the army on the hills above the village."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Bouckaert, that he didn't claim or didn't tell the Prosecutor that he had seen his sons climb out of the window, unlike what he did with you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say to us that he saw them climb out of the window. He said when the fire started, the boys climbed out through the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, that suggests, doesn't it, that he saw that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be read either way, can't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it can. Who else could have told him that they had climbed out of the windows?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, this seems to be disintegrating now into simply argument. I would suggest this not helpful to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Saxon. Carry on, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir? We really need to try to have short answers, and I think those can be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, you're getting short answers, but you're giving terribly long questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Bouckaert, that Mr. Jashari did not tell the Prosecution that he had seen his son climb out of the windows, unlike what he had done with you?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: No, he didn't?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he didn't tell us that he saw his sons climbing out of the windows. He said, "When the fire started, the boys climbed through the window." That doesn't mean that he saw them. It could have -- even in his statement, he said they either burned in the house or they climbed out of the window and were shot, or whatever he says, so obviously, since he found the bodies later, it was a fair conclusion to make that they climbed out of the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But is that correct, sir, that the only way in which he could have had that knowledge was by having witnessed that particular incident, since he indicated to you that no one was with him at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I disagree. I mean, I think his statement is clear. He says "When the fire started, the boys climbed out through the window. They ran away, but the police started shooting at them."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that he did not claim to the Prosecution that he saw them run away; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, I don't know exactly what you're trying to get at. I think he left his sons in the house. He came back later and found them dead. He knew the police had been at his house, and he told us that his sons had climbed out of the window, that they had tried to run away and were shot down. I think it's a perfectly logical conclusion to make, and it doesn't suggest -- he doesn't suggest in the statement, in the report, that he had personally witnessed these things. He could just as well have concluded them from what he found just minutes afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But he didn't say that to the Prosecution; correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say what?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: He didn't say that he had seen his sons run away from the house?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And as I've said time and time again, neither did he say that to us. He said that the boys had run away. He did not say, "I saw the boys climb out of the window and run away."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpretation kindly ask you to slow down and make pauses.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct also that he didn't claim to have seen four or five policemen walk up to the three men in the field; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he didn't claim that to us or to --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: To the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't know -- I'd have to read his entire statement to say -- see whether he claimed it or not. I mean, you read some specific passages, but unless I'm familiar with the entire statement, how can I make that -- answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, from what I've read to you, is that correct that when he came out of the bushes, he did not know whether they had been killed or whether they had run away? That's what he said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and in paragraph 45 he also says: "Also beside Kadri we found some papers which indicate that the bodies were searched." So, again, I think it's a logical conclusion for him to make that some police had walked up to the bodies, since they had been --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Let's just stick with the questions of the four and five policemen. Is that correct that when he came out of the bushes, he didn't know what had happened to his children, whether they were alive or dead; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that indicates, doesn't it, that he didn't know or he didn't claim, in any case, that he had witnessed anyone killing his children; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you seek to interview any policemen or any member of the Ministry of Interior to verify this story about -- from Mr. Jashari?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you visit the location where the three individuals had been shot?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you look for bullet casings around the area where Mr. Jashari said his son had been shot at close range?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you find any?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't find any.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown once again what is Exhibit 1D24. Mr. Bouckaert, that's the same OSCE report that I have shown you -- that I have shown you earlier. And I'll ask the Registry to go to page 4 directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'll ask you to look at the second paragraphs. That's the paragraph starting with: "There were no bullet casings ..." This is the conclusions of the OSCE after their visit on the 14th: "There were no bullet casings found near the three men located in the field or on the hillside leading to their bodies. There were no superficial indications that they were shot at close range. From the totality of the circumstances at the scene, it appeared the men were shot from a distance while running uphill." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you did not have that information at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you have indicated to me earlier that you had had the benefit of the notes, I believe, of Nicholas Wood, a journalist; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He had been with the OSCE observer at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you make a reference to those notes in your report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 11 again of Mr. Bouckaert's report. It's P352 and go to page 11. And if I could ask the Registry to focus on the paragraph starting with: "The bodies of Bajram Jashari ..." It's the bulky paragraph in the middle. I'd like to read a sentence which you referred to -- where you gave a reference to the notes of Mr. Wood. It says: "25-year-old Xhelal Bajrami's body had multiple gunshot wounds in the back, the buttocks, and the back of his legs, suggesting he was shot in the back while running away. The body of 31-year-old Kadri Jashari was found a few metres farther away from the house of Qani Jashari. His body showed several large exit wounds on the upper front of the chest and his neck, suggesting again that he had been shot in the back while running away." Then he says: "According to his family, Kadri had just returned 10 days before from working in Austria." Is that correct, Mr. Bouckaert, that the information which Mr. Wood provided to you suggests that Mr. Jashari, Kadri Jashari, was shot and killed by bullets shot in the back and not in the front; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would be inconsistent with the version given by Qani Jashari to you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were unable to confirm that part of Mr. Jashari's story, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you published it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I understand that you had no reason, and I think you've indicated, that you had no reason to doubt the reliability of Mr. Qani Jashari at the time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in your statement, at paragraph 82 you indicate that as a professional investigator, you have been trained to assess the credibility of witnesses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And did you inquire with anyone whether -- any of the villagers, for instance, whether you should handle the information provided by you from Mr. Jashari with some care; did you make that inquiry?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask any of the other villagers about the reliability of Mr. Jashari, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could we move, Your Honour, for a minute in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Bouckaert, that you did not make any inquiry about the reliability, in general, or in this particular instance, about the information provided to you by Mr. Jashari?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I interviewed him, Mr. Jashari was a credible and lucid witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you a number of questions about another witness which -- or another person which you interviewed, and that's Mr. Elmaz Jusufi. Do you recall interviewing Mr. Jusufi?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that the interview of Mr. Jusufi took place in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall if and whether he had told you when he had left the village after the incident?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: I would like to go back to what is P352; that is, the report of Mr. Bouckaert and ask that the Registry should turn at page 7 of the report. Mr. Bouckaert, if you can focus on the top of the page, that's the first full paragraph, if you want, which starts with the words: "Elmaz Jusufi ..." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you said the following: "Elmaz Jusufi's home was among the first to be attacked. Elmaz Jusufi, a 58-year-old bedridden paraplegic, told Human Rights Watch how the Macedonian police forces blew away the gate of his home, shot dead his 33-year-old son Rami Jusufi through the front door of the home, and then torched his car." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: M'mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And then there's a quote which is indented, which comes from the interview of Mr. Jusufi. That's Footnote 14, and it says this: "The moment the attack on the village started, they came to my house. My front yard was full of them. There were about 20. They were all in uniform, but not masked. They bombed the gate to the yard. Then my son went to close the front door. At the moment he closed the door and went back into the room. There was a huge explosion. They blew away the door with machine-gun fire. That was the moment my son was hit in the side and stomach from the shots. He fell down there. It happened right in front of my eyes." Then he goes on to say: "The police did not come into the house. I got into my wheelchair and went close to the door and my son. My son was suffering for about two hours. He was in a lot of pain. My car was parked in the front yard, right next to the gate. They poured gasoline on it and set it on fire. I heard the police say, 'Pour the gasoline.'" Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct, that -- and I will come back to the second person, but you relied upon the evidence given to you by Mr. Muzafer Jusufi in corroboration of the information you received from Elmaz Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And the evidence which you -- or the information which you recorded from Mr. Rami Jusufi was that his son had --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rami Jusufi was shot. You mean Elmaz Jusufi.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, I'm grateful. The information which you recorded from Elmaz Jusufi was that his son had closed the door and then went back into the house, and then there was a huge explosion, and he was hit and killed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I understood, he was in the process of closing the door, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And he died some two hours later; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: On the 8th of May of this year, Mr. Jusufi was read that passage in court, that record of the information which you provided in your statement. And it's -- Your Honour, it's the transcript of the 8th of May, 2007, page 508 to 509. This is the question: "In this report," and this is talking about your report, "it is stated this is a statement that you made on the 20th of August, 2001, as it is stated in the report itself, immediately after the events. You stated the following ..." And then a passage of your report is being read: "At the moment when the attack started, they came to my house. My yard was full. There were about 20 of them there. They were all wearing uniforms, but not masks as well. They shelled the gate to the yard. My son went to close the front door. At the moment when he closed the door and returned back to the room, there was a big blast. They demolished the door by -- they blew up the door by machine-gun." And this is the answer of Mr. Jusufi: "This is a mistake. This is a total and complete mistake." So do you agree that Mr. Jusufi did not adopt that particular version which was given in your report when he gave evidence in court here?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without seeing the full statement of Mr. Jusufi's answer, I don't know what -- what mistake he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, what he said there after is this: "So you've tried to interrupt me, stating that this was not true; is that correct?" And then he answers: "What you read in the beginning, that is not correct. It is correct that he was killed while at the gate, but it's not correct that he went outside and then came back in." And then there's a question: "So if Human Rights Watch wrote what I just read, you are saying that they did not relay correctly what has happened and what you have told them; is that correct?" And then he says: "Partially it is correct, but there's a part that is incorrect. The part that describes how he was killed near the entrance door, that is correct, but the part that was saying that he left and then came back, that is not correct. As he was going to close the door, that's when he was killed."

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I would just like to object to the unethical nature of this cross-examination. If you compare the statement which is in the report, it's exactly what Mr. Jusufi confirmed. Counsel was trying to mislead me into making a miss -- which is obviously due to a translation error as he was being cross-examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This was the assessment of Mr. Jusufi --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because he objected to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please make pauses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux, Mr. Bouckaert has put his finger on a problem with the way you took an answer in the evidence and what that is based upon. The answer you attributed to something or gave to it, in effect, quite different from that which was intended by the witness on the face of the evidence. So instead of arguing what it may have meant or didn't mean, which is taking a lot of time and which is not really going to advance this Tribunal, you can certainly put to the witness, as you have been, a different account that was given on key points and have the witness acknowledge that that is different from what he was told. There's little point in having the witness then debate with you time and again what the differences were or might have been or what their explanation might be. If they're different, they're different. Whether the witness then explored, by way of seeking confirmation, what was told him, I think he's made it clear to you what he did and didn't do about that. The witness, of course, did not have subsequent OTP statements, did not have evidence given in this trial by these people, so the value of what you're putting is really in the fact that he was told one account and a different account is given by the same person at another time. That's the value. That's the point you need to make and can make it much more quickly than you are and then you can move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, in this case the witness was asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We fully appreciate that, Mr. Bouckaert. But as you will see, we do not interfere with counsel a lot, and I made it quite clear at the beginning of my comments --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- to counsel that we saw the point that you are making and accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply for the witness, there was no intent to mislead him in any way. The entire page was to be read, as it has been, although the witness wanted -- I mean, I'm going to ask that first, where it came from and it was read in advance. Mr. Bouckaert can be reassured that the entire passage was to be read to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: You've indicated yesterday in your evidence that you recalled having seen blood inside the house of Mr. Jusufi. Can you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you recall where exactly inside the house that pool of blood which you describe had been?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall seeing a pool of blood about one metre inside the house away from the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 197, and it has an ERN of N001-4925-07. If it could be enlarged a bit for Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the entrance of the house of Mr. Jusufi on this picture?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: If the bottom of the picture could be enlarged somewhat, I would be grateful, and if, Mr. Bouckaert, you could indicate where, in that entrance, you recall having seen a pool of blood. Could the -- I would ask for the assistance of the usher, perhaps, to help Mr. Bouckaert.

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And on that picture, Mr. Bouckaert, can you locate any pool of blood or any marking?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to tell from this picture, but that's the approximate place where I noticed blood on the carpet.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We would seek to tender this document, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D92, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And simply for clarification, Mr. Bouckaert, you've indicated yesterday that you did not take any picture from the inside of the house, I think you said. You said that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Is that a picture which you took, the present picture?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume it is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll ask also that the picture be admitted under seal. We understand the person on picture may be protected, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't quite grasp that last comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: We believe that the person on the picture may be a protected witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be under seal. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the first break and resume at a quarter past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. Hopefully, you won't receive a phone call --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I turned it off.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, I'd like to show you another picture, which is P-5, which you had been shown by the Prosecution yesterday. Mr. Bouckaert, do you recall being shown this picture by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And it's one of the pictures that you, yourself, took; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can enlarge a bit the bottom of the picture, the last third of it. Further down, further down. Well, thank you. And here, Mr. Bouckaert, you had indicated that when you took that picture, you found those casings which were -- bullet casings which were there on the ground; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And if we can simply go back to the normal size of the picture, please. Is that correct that more or less on the extreme left of the picture, there was a wall there, Mr. Bouckaert, that is, that approximately between, I would say, 30 to 60 centimetres from the bullets, if one goes to the left, there was a wall there; is? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I will take your word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But can you recall that there was indeed a wall there that continues from this part?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I honestly don't recall, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And would you agree that this casing -- bullet casings which you see on this picture and which you saw at the time are of the 7.62-millimetre type; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct also that this is the sort of ammunition which is used, among other things, with Kalashnikov weapons?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And perhaps I should ask you this, but have you ever, yourself, shot from a Kalashnikov weapon or seen anyone seen from a Kalashnikov weapon?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the answer is "yes" to both.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that correct that when you shoot with a Kalashnikov weapon, the bullet or, rather, the casing of the bullet is projected on the right side of the gun; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: In fact, the projection is towards forwards and to the right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And is that also correct that the projection of the bullet or the casing of the bullet has an ejection projection of two to three metres from --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: -- from the gun; is that correct? Thank you. I'd like to move on now to another witness, which -- we can remove the picture from the screen. I'm grateful. I'd like to ask you a number of questions about another individual and another villager which you interviewed during your investigation, and that's Mr. Muzafer Jusufi. Do you recall interviewing Mr. Jusufi?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall Mr. Jusufi telling you that as Mr. Elmaz Jusufi had said, he had witnessed what he said was the killing of Rami Jusufi; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And I would just like to read the information in the report, sir, which you recorded. It's at page 7, Your Honour, of P352. Mr. Bouckaert, this is again your report. It is the section which starts in the middle of the page with the words: "Muzafer Jusufi ..." If the Registry could enlarge somewhat the document for Mr. Bouckaert. I'll read out the quote which you have recorded Mr. Jusufi -- the information which you recorded Mr. Jusufi to tell -- to give you: "The firing started and I went to see Elmaz. A very short time later, heavy firing started all around the village. After two seconds, the gate to the front yard was blown up either from a grenade or an RPG, a rocket-propelled grenade. I don't know. Immediately, they came inside the front yard. Then they shot a burst at the car. One of them shouted, 'Give me the gasoline.' They set the car on fire with the gasoline. Then they came towards the entrance to the house. They started shooting automatic bursts in our direction. Rami Jusufi was locking the door, and after he locked the door, he was shot. There were a lot of police officers, maybe 15 or 20. After one and a half to two hours, the boy died. The police did not come in. They just stood at the door. They were swearing at us all the time." And then there's an expletive. Do you recall Mr. Muzafer Jusufi telling you that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, it's very difficult for me to recall directly, but if there is -- if it's in the report, I certainly interviewed him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as you just pointed out, it was --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Yes, he had told you that he had witnessed the killing of Mr. Rami Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that was the corroboration of the evidence of Elmaz Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, together with our physical inspection.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown what is Rule 65 ter 1D14. It's at ERN 1D00-0183, I'm sorry, and there is no Macedonian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Mr. Bouckaert, this is again a statement of Mr. Jusufi or Jusufovski Muzafer which he gave to the Prosecution on the 12th of October of 2005, and I ask the Registry to go to page 3 of that statement, please. And I'll ask, Mr. Bouckaert, that you focus on paragraph 9 of Mr. Jusufi's statement. I'll read it out to you. He said this to the Prosecution: "On the question of killing of Rami Jusufi, I wish to state that I was hiding in the room and did not see what happened. When the police left the house, I came out from where I was hiding and found Rami Jusufi covered with blood and barely alive. Rami Jusufi died shortly after he was laid on the couch." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that would suggest that, in fact, if this statement is to be believed, Mr. Jusufi did not see the killing of Mr. Rami Jusufi; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what the paragraph suggests. I'm not sure if -- yeah, I'm not sure why he's stated this in his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Thank you. If I can ask you another question about another witness which you've interviewed, Mr. Bouckaert. That is Mr. Aziz Bajrami. Do you recall interviewing Mr. Aziz Bajrami? And I can draw your attention perhaps --

utterances.speaker: PETER BOUCKAERT [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I interviewed Mr. Bajrami on two separate occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
